product-features.summary: Pick the Claude.ai feature that matches the job: Projects for recurring context, Research for sourced multi-step web work, artifacts for documents, tables and small tools, plain chat for one-off questions.
points: Projects are self-contained workspaces with their own chat history, uploaded knowledge and custom instructions. Knowledge and instructions persist across every chat inside the Project, so recurring context (style guides, handbooks, client briefs, comparison rules) belongs there rather than in every prompt.

On paid plans, when Project knowledge approaches the context limit Claude switches to retrieval (RAG) and loads only the relevant parts of the knowledge for each question, so a Project can hold far more than a single conversation.

Research runs multiple searches that build on each other, across the web and connected sources such as Gmail, Google Calendar and Google Docs, and returns a report with easy-to-check citations. Use it for comprehensive, sourced, multi-step information gathering (competitor comparisons, updating internal documents with current external facts). It requires web search to be on and is on paid plans.
Plain web search is for a quick current fact; extended thinking is for harder reasoning without external sources; Research is for gathering and synthesising across many sources. They can be combined.

Artifacts are what Claude makes that you would put in front of someone: documents, tables, code, diagrams, single-page web tools, dashboards. Claude creates them for significant, self-contained content (typically over 15 lines) that you will edit, iterate on or reuse outside the conversation. They can be edited in place, versioned and published.
Artifacts are outputs, not storage: they do not carry context into future chats. Persisting context is a Project's job.
Plain chat is right for one-off questions and short answers; an artifact for a one-line fact or a Project for a single question is overhead without benefit.

Features combine: run Research inside a Project so current external facts are compared against persistent internal knowledge; build the deliverable as an artifact in the same Project so it is versioned and shared context.
Memory records preferences and working context, not verbatim documents; it is not a substitute for Project knowledge when a specific file must be consulted.

Common distractors: pasting the same document into every chat; keeping one chat open indefinitely; using Research to "look up" your own internal document; expecting an artifact to persist context; relying on memory to hold a 90-page handbook.

model-types.summary: Distinguish the Haiku, Sonnet and Opus tiers by their speed-versus-depth trade-off and know how switching between them behaves.
points: Haiku is the fastest, lightest tier: suited to quick lookups, simple edits, classification and high-volume straightforward tasks where speed and efficiency matter more than reasoning depth.
Sonnet is the balanced everyday model: fast and highly capable, designed for the vast majority of writing, analysis, question-answering and coding-help tasks. It is the sensible default.
Opus is the most capable tier for genuinely complex, multi-step problems with interacting constraints, used when quality matters more than speed or volume.
Describe the tiers by trade-off (speed and efficiency versus reasoning depth), not by price; exam items avoid pricing specifics.

Switch models by clicking the model name next to the send button. Switching mid-conversation keeps the history; the new model sees everything the previous one produced, and the change applies from the next response.
The picker remembers your last selection by default, and organisations can set a default model; a default is a convenience, not a recommendation for a given task.
Effort and extended thinking are settings, not tiers: they make a model work harder on a response (more thorough, slower, more usage). They do not turn the lightest tier into the best reasoner.
No tier is infallible. A more capable model reduces error rates but every model can produce plausible wrong details, so verification is still required.
Haiku follows instructions and produces structured output (tables, JSON-like lists); its limitation is depth on hard problems, not formatting.
Model tier does not govern memory across chats; that comes from the memory feature, Projects and chat search.
Common distractors: reversing the tiers; "Sonnet is only for code"; "bigger model remembers more between chats"; one bad result on a hard task used to justify moving all work to the heaviest tier.

model-fit.summary: Choose the model tier by weighing the task's real requirements for quality, speed and cost, and prefer the least expensive tier that meets the quality bar.
points: Start from the task, not the tier. Ask: how hard is the reasoning, how costly is an error, how many items, how fast is it needed?
Simple, high-volume, time-boxed work (short summaries, tagging, subject-line rewrites, routing tickets) fits the fastest tier; the most capable tier there wastes time and usage for no visible gain.
One-off, high-stakes, multi-constraint reasoning (an acquisition recommendation, a five-year strategy) fits the most capable tier; speed and volume are irrelevant and the cost of an error dominates.
Mixed everyday workloads fit the balanced tier as a default, stepping up to the most capable tier only for the occasional unusually hard problem.
Fit the model to each step of a process rather than the whole process: fastest for the bulk classification step, balanced for ordinary drafting, most capable for the single strategic analysis.
Consistency of style comes from instructions and examples, not from using one tier everywhere.

Make the decision with evidence when stakes are high: run the candidate tiers on a representative test set, pick the cheapest and fastest one that meets the required accuracy, and re-test when the inputs (such as a handbook) change.
Adding "be extremely careful" to instructions does not close a measured accuracy gap; a stated correctness requirement rules out a tier that misses it, however fast.
Effort and extended thinking add per-response time and usage; they suit hard problems, not bulk simple work under a deadline.

The official sample question for this skill keys the faster, lower-cost model for high-volume short customer replies; always using the top model, disabling features or switching platforms are the distractors.
Common distractors: "volume deserves the top model"; "the top tier never needs checking"; "use the default until it fails" on a costly one-off; alternating tiers item by item.

context-limits.summary: Understand that each chat starts fresh and that long chats degrade, and know when to restart with a summary, persist context in a Project or memory, or move large material into Project knowledge.
points: The context window is Claude's working memory for one conversation. A portion is reserved for the response, and once a conversation approaches the limit Claude tells you; the remedy is to start a new conversation or use a Project.

Claude does not carry one chat's content into another by itself. Without a persistence feature, each chat starts fresh; "same tone as yesterday" only works if yesterday's draft is pasted, stored in a Project, or covered by memory or chat search.
Long conversations get slower, consume more usage and become less reliable as early details are crowded out or contradicted. Restating decisions in every message makes the problem worse.

Restart pattern: ask Claude to summarise the decisions, open questions and constraints so far, then seed a new chat (or a Project) with that summary. Summaries carry state; they should not replace reference documents that need detail.
Persist pattern: put recurring context (client background, report structure, style rules, handbooks) into Project instructions and knowledge so every chat in the Project sees it.

For material larger than a conversation can hold, add it as Project knowledge; on paid plans retrieval loads only the relevant portions for each question. Splitting files across parallel chats or shrinking them to a one-page summary loses cross-references or detail.

Memory (on by default for Free, Pro and Max; off by default for Team and Enterprise until an owner enables it) saves context about your role, preferences and ongoing work, organised as topics you can view, edit or delete in Settings. Each Project has its own memory space. Incognito chats are not saved to memory or history.
Chat search lets Claude find and reuse past conversations when asked ("what did we decide about X?") on plans that include it; it is a retrieval step, not automatic recall.
Memory is for preferences and working context, not verbatim documents; it will not store a 300-page procedure set or six syllabi word for word.

Automatic context management can summarise earlier messages as a chat nears its limit; it keeps the conversation going but uses more of your usage allowance, so restarting or using a Project is still the efficient choice.
Model tier does not change what is remembered across chats or add room to a chat at its limit.

Common distractors: "switch to a bigger model so it can reach further back"; "tell Claude to remember harder"; "turn on memory so it memorises the documents"; "keep one enormous chat per client"; "give the chat a good title so Claude can reuse it".
